item.title: Freedom of expression is not a privilege granted by those in power. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
The concerns raised by rights organizations and media advocates over the proposed changes to the Cyber Protection Act, 2026, deserve serious consideration. We agree that the government must recognize that any legislation intended to protect cyberspace must not become a tool for silencing dissent.
The proposed provisions concerning defamation, maligning, rumours, and misinformation are particularly worrying because vague definitions can easily be misused. When the law leaves too much room for interpretation, legitimate criticism, investigative journalism, and public-interest reporting may become grounds for legal harassment.
The possibility of arbitrary content restrictions and punitive action against media outlets makes these concerns even more pressing.
Bangladesh has already witnessed how cyber laws can be weaponized against journalists, critics, and ordinary citizens. We cannot allow a new legal framework to reproduce the same failures under a different name.
Changing governments must also mean changing the practices that undermine democratic rights. Otherwise, promises of reform amount to little more than rhetoric.
There is, of course, a need to address genuine cybercrime, online harassment, and other harmful activities, but these objectives must be pursued through clearly defined offences, due process, independent oversight, and meaningful safeguards for freedom of expression.
The government must consult journalists, legal experts, civil society organizations, and digital rights advocates before advancing legislation that affects the fundamental rights of millions.
More importantly, any and all further attempts to stifle our freedom of speech must be dealt with promptly and decisively. This requires more than assurances that a law will not be misused -- it requires enforceable protections, transparent procedures, and accountability whenever authorities overstep their powers.
Freedom of expression is not a privilege granted by those in power. It is a fundamental right that allows citizens to question authority and hold institutions accountable.
It's time the government shows us that it understands this distinction. We cannot keep repeating the same mistakes at the cost of our freedom of speech.

item.title: The rule of law cannot depend on who holds a weapon. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
State Minister Ishraque Hossain’s decision to resign -- following public outrage over footage of him brandishing a firearm during an anti-drug operation -- is an important development. However, his resignation must not be allowed to end the dialogue about his conduct or the responsibilities of elected representatives.
Let us be clear: Ishraque's actions were not part of a minister’s role, and under no circumstances can they be misconstrued as valid or acceptable.
Ministers are entrusted with political leadership and the responsibility of ensuring that state institutions function effectively. An elected government must strengthen relevant agencies, provide them with adequate resources, ensure that they can perform their duties without political interference, as well as hold them accountable if they fail to do so.
It must be understood: We have not elected MPs to take the law into their own hands, nor should the public be encouraged to view such conduct as a heroic demonstration of strength.
Allowing elected officials to assume law enforcement roles risks undermining established procedures, weakening institutional authority, and setting a dangerous precedent. The rule of law cannot depend on who holds a weapon or occupies a position of power.
Drug trafficking is most certainly a serious problem that demands sustained action. However, an effective anti-drug campaign must be conducted through lawful procedures, professional investigations, and accountable enforcement.
No individual, regardless of political position or stated intentions, should be exempt from these standards.
Ishraque’s resignation must also not be taken as a substitute for accountability. The circumstances surrounding the incident must be examined, and any violation must be addressed through due process.
Such conduct cannot be praised as decisive leadership or ignored because its stated objective is an important one.
Strong institutions, not individual displays of power, are what protect the public and build trust in the state. The government must demonstrate that elected representatives are expected to uphold the law, not bypass it.

item.title: In art, a wall of heritage and an artificial message of division. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
Even before Bangladesh was born as an independent state, the country’s cultural arena has been a battleground. This fight is not waged with shields and swords. It has mainly been carried on through the narrative of “religion versus culture.” Should the ancient culture of the Bengali people, which bears the strong influence of Sanatani (Hindu), Buddhist and Islamic faiths, be the foundation of national and state identity in this land? Or should the character of this state rest only on the religious identity of its Muslim-majority citizens, where language and culture from the Arab-Persian region count for more than Bengal’s own culture?
There is no reason to doubt the narrow communal mindset hidden inside this debate and this division, and these days it is hardly hidden at all. It is also undeniable that this debate plays an important role in Bangladesh’s political divisions. Above all, it was through this very division that attempts were made in 1970 and 1971 to block the emergence of Bangladesh as an independent country. But the 1970 election and the Liberation War of 1971 defeated that effort, and Bangladesh was born on the basis of Bengali cultural identity.
Recent events show that the stirring-up of the country’s origin, identity and basis of existence through that narrow debate, which began after the 2024 change of power, has not yet died down. The anti-Liberation War mindset that raised its head under the interim Yunus government is now being revived. Those who destroyed the Sheikh Mujib Memorial Museum at Road 32 in Dhanmondi to erase the history of the Liberation War, and who vandalized sculptures related to Bangabandhu and the Liberation War across the country, are now trying to strike at the very foundation of independence by a new route.
Distortion of history
Recently, the walls along a road in Dhaka were decorated with portraits of some leading figures of Bengali culture. Many welcomed this initiative by the city authorities on the wall beside the Shilpakala Academy. But then a campaign began on social media whose language, underlying message and purpose have become very familiar since the 2024 uprising. However crude the campaign’s methods, its aim is clear: T o crack the country’s cultural identity, to create division on the basis of religion, and to move the country’s birth from 1971 back to 1947, presenting Bangladesh as a product of the “two-nation theory.”
Freedom of dissent is important in every democratic society, even when that dissent amounts to distorting history. But it would be wrong to call what has been going on in Bangladesh for the past two years merely free expression. Alongside the rewriting of the nation’s history, there has been destructive activity, extreme intolerance of and threats against the pro-Liberation War narrative, and even communally provocative statements.
Some people on social media have asked why portraits of Satyajit Ray or Ishwar Chandra Vidyasagar were placed beside those of Bangladesh’s eminent artist Zainul Abedin, the actor Humayun Faridi or the national poet Kazi Nazrul Islam. Their argument is that Ray and Vidyasagar are not “Bangladeshi.” Those who say this surely understand very well that “Bangladeshi” identity is not the point here. These figures were chosen for their mountainous contributions to Bengali culture. That is exactly their problem. But there, communalism is visibly playing a big part.
Nazrul and the nation
For example, there is no fuss about the portrait of Kazi Nazrul Islam, Bangladesh’s national poet. There is no reason for any. Just as there should be no controversy over Ishwar Chandra Vidyasagar, there should be no objection to Nazrul either, because both are Bengali and both made extraordinary contributions to Bengali literature and culture. Like Vidyasagar, Kazi Nazrul Islam was also an Indian. So why object to one of them? Because he is Hindu?
Bangabandhu Sheikh Mujibur Rahman brought Nazrul to Bangladesh in 1972 and allotted a house in Dhanmondi for his whole family. Nazrul was not only a leading figure in Bengali-language literature; in the backdrop of the Liberation War, he was a source of inspiration for the people. Nazrul’s poems and songs gave the people courage and inspiration in 1971. After independence, the government of independent Bangladesh felt fulfilled at being able to bring him close, and the people were happy and proud to see him with their own eyes.
The tragedy was that Nazrul had lost his understanding and his speech many years before coming to Dhaka. How much he understood that he had come to Dhaka as a guest of a newly independent state is open to question. But it was probably because of the state honour he received in Dhaka that Nazrul’s family stayed on in Bangladesh.
Nazrul was born in India, spent his whole life in India, and was an Indian. He did not become a Bangladeshi overnight by spending the last four years of his life in Dhaka. Yet there is no controversy or question anywhere about declaring Nazrul the national poet of Bangladesh. There should not be. Likewise, there should be no question or controversy about adopting a song written by Rabindranath Tagore as the national anthem. But here too, out of exactly the same communal mindset, controversy has been created over Rabindranath, a follower of the Brahmo Samaj, and over his song “Amar Shonar Bangla.”
The drama and the police response
A drama of erasing Rabindranath’s portrait from the wall of the Shilpakala Academy was also staged recently. It has to be called a drama because, while a woman was about to deface Rabindranath’s portrait with ink, countless people were seen around her filming on their phones, and perhaps one or two were even live-streaming. At that very moment, a policeman ran up and stopped her!
The whole incident looked like a publicity stunt. But afterwards the police filed a “sedition” case against the woman and four people from her organization , arranging even more publicity for them. The communal mindset of an organization that exists in name only, expressed through vandalism, may be seen as a nuisance. But whether it is reasonable to treat it as outright “sedition” is a question that can certainly be asked.
Yet there is also a silver lining behind the dark cloud. On one hand, the police reaction seems excessive, especially when the alleged “crime” is essentially confined to a political statement. On the other hand, the authorities’ firmness deserves praise. Had the same incident happened under the Yunus government, the portraits of Satyajit Ray and Ishwar Chandra Vidyasagar might have been wiped off the Shilpakala Academy wall overnight. Perhaps the officials in charge at the city authority would have had to answer for it, and perhaps a job or two would have been at stake.
It goes without saying that the course of events will not stop here. The process of cutting the people of Bangladesh off from their cultural history and heritage, which began two years ago, will undoubtedly continue. Whether the government will confront this tendency, or stay indifferent like the Yunus government and in effect keep encouraging it, is a decision the BNP must make.
Instead of isolated reactions to isolated incidents and overreactions like the “sedition” case, it is time for the government to send a clear message. The foundation of Bangladesh’s birth is the language and culture of Bengalis irrespective of religion or caste. In the Bengali language, literature and the whole cultural arena, no division on the basis of religion, or of which side of the border someone was born on, is acceptable. The government must give this message clearly. Otherwise the possibility will remain that this artificial division turns into political, social and communal conflict.
Sabir Mustafa is the former head of BBC Bangla and is currently working as a freelance journalist and podcaster. Views expressed are the author’s own.

item.title: Bangladesh seeks answers after Saudi Arabia executes two of its citizens without notice. [ middleeasteye ]
item.description:
Bangladesh seeks answers after Saudi Arabia executes two of its citizens without notice

Submitted by Areeb Ullah on Mon, 10/19/2026 - 12:59
Dhaka said it was not informed by Saudi Arabia that it had executed the pair arrested in Mecca for 'indecent acts'
Bangladeshi workers sitting outside an airport after flights to Saudi Arabia were cancelled following a series of Houthi attacks in October (AFP/Piyas Biswas)
Off

Bangladesh is seeking answers on why Saudi Arabia executed two Bangladeshi nationals in the holy city of Mecca without telling Dhaka.

Last week, Saudi Arabia executed a male and a female Bangladeshi national after they were convicted of committing “indecent acts” inside a mosque.

Riyadh did not provide further details on the acts the two Bangladeshi nationals allegedly committed or whether they had legal representation in the Gulf kingdom, according to local media reports.

Reacting to the incident, Bangladesh’s minister for foreign affairs, Humaiun Kobir, told reporters that he was “very disappointed” by the lack of communication and that Dhaka was seeking an explanation on why they were executed and not informed beforehand about the execution.

“We have sought an explanation from our friendly bilateral partner to look into the matter and know why the gap in information sharing and exchanges happened here. We are in discussions," he told reporters at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs on Monday.

Earlier, the Bangladeshi foreign ministry said that it was waiting for a copy of the full verdict and the circumstances that led to the execution.

The official added that the two executed Bangladeshis were included in a list of prisoners that Saudi Arabia had shared with Bangladesh but did not indicate that they had planned to execute them.

Soundstorm: Why are DJs flocking to play in Saudi Arabia’s music festival?
Read More »

Last week, Saudi Arabia’s Supreme Court overturned the death sentence of a Sri Lankan national after he allegedly insulted Islam and the Prophet Muhammad.

Sri Lanka’s Deputy Foreign Minister Arun Hemachandra confirmed that Riyadh had overturned the death sentence of Anojan Sivarasa.

The 27-year-old remains imprisoned after he was sentenced to five years in prison and fined three million Saudi Riyals ($800,000).

The court handed down the sentence amid intense criticism of Riyadh's legal system.

Saudi Arabia relies on interpretations of Islamic law, alongside cybercrime and counterterror legislation, to target online expression under the guise of protecting "public morals".

This has resulted in a surge of decades-long prison terms for social media users and an increased use of capital punishment.

At least 175 people have been executed so far this year, the majority of whom are foreign nationals.
